common_name: Lily Pads Giant Evergreen Solomon's Seal

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring; establishes slowly into a spreading patch over several years.

directions: This recently collected, not-yet-formally-described Chinese Disporopsis forms broad, glossy evergreen leaves well over twice the size of common Solomon's seal relatives, with small brown-speckled yellow flowers tucked along the stems in spring. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil and give it years to spread by rhizome into an impressively lush patch. Because the foliage is evergreen, it earns its keep as a textural anchor in the winter shade garden where most perennial companions have died back.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall or as container stock in spring; emerges and flowers in mid-spring.

directions: This Hans Hansen selection of the Japanese jack-in-the-pulpit subspecies urashima carries striking silvery banding down each lobe of its horseshoe-shaped leaf, setting it apart from the plain-leaved typical form. In mid-spring it sends up a near-black hooded flower with a white throat and a long whip-like appendage trailing from the spathe. Grow in humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil with part sun to light shade, and let the tuber go dormant undisturbed through summer dry spells.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into consistently moist soil.

directions: A 2021 Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction named for Tennessee plantsman Robert Wilson, this ligularia forms a compact, bold-textured clump of deeply cut, glossy green foliage that stays tidier than many larger ligularia selections. In early summer it sends up sturdy flower spikes topped with clusters of golden-orange daisies roughly 3.5 inches across that draw pollinators to the shade border. Keep the soil evenly moist to boggy, since like all ligularias the broad leaves wilt fast if the ground dries out or afternoon sun hits them directly.

common_name: Snow Globe Dwarf Striped Mondo Grass

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring, set close together for faster carpet coverage.

directions: A miniature striped mondo grass shared by plantsman Darrell Probst from Japan, each tiny rosette measures barely two inches across with leaves pinstriped in dark green and creamy white, slowly knitting together into a dense, low carpet. It is among the smallest mondo grass selections in cultivation, so patience and tight initial spacing pay off when using it as a groundcover between stepping stones or at the front of a shaded border. Grow in part sun to shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring; spreads gradually by short rhizomes into a solid mat.

directions: Kokuryu is a Japanese black mondo grass clone traded under its own name in the nursery trade, with threadlike quarter-inch-wide foliage so dark it reads as true black rather than purple-black in most light; some sources treat it as effectively the same clone as the better-known 'Nigrescens', so expect similar performance either way. Plants form tidy circular mounds that gradually knit together via rhizomes into a slowly expanding mat, useful as a dramatic dark accent against pale gravel or stone. Grow in part sun to shade in well-drained soil with regular moisture.

common_name: Tears of Gold Variegated Mondo Grass

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into evenly moist, well-drained soil.

directions: This narrow-leaved mondo grass selection carries fine vertical gold streaking down leaves about half the width of the typical species, with occasional all-green or all-gold blades appearing within the same clump for extra textural variety. It stays low and slowly spreads into a fine-textured mat, working well as a bright edging plant along shaded paths. Grow in part sun to shade in consistently moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring; spreads gradually, reaching a substantial patch after about five years in good soil.

directions: A variegated mondo grass in cultivation since the late 1990s, with narrow leaves finely striped in white, giving established clumps a frosted look even from a distance. It is a moderate, steady spreader rather than an explosively fast one, reaching several feet across only after a number of years in good soil, making it a practical choice for covering ground under trees where turf struggles. Grow in part sun to shade in moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or plugs in spring; useful for tight spots between pavers.

directions: Originating at Bluebird Nursery, this extremely compact dwarf mondo grass forms tight, rounded green clumps so uniform they resemble golf balls scattered across wet grass. Its diminutive scale makes it ideal for miniature or trough gardens, moss-garden accents, and narrow joints between shaded paving stones where larger grasses would overwhelm the space. Grow in part sun to shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Among the most recognizable leopard plant selections, its large rounded leaves curl at the base in overlapping lobes that create a distinctive spiral reminiscent of a snail's shell. The bold, glossy clump makes a strong architectural statement in a shaded border and pairs well with ferns and fine-textured companions needing similar moisture. Keep soil consistently moist, since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry spells, and give winter protection at the colder end of its hardiness range.
